What makes him Descartes rather than someone else is a particular way of living. He not only thinks; he also writes and publishes what he writes.
Why does he live in this way rather than another?
Why does he not merely think, but also put his thoughts on paper?
Why does he not merely write them down, but publish them?
Why does he publish some manuscripts and burn others?
We have to admit that his reflections on himself—or rather, on the “thinking thing”—give us no answer to any of these questions.

The definition of the human I as a thinking thing is therefore plainly inadequate from a philosophical point of view. It cannot answer the questions we can ask a philosopher about his life and activity in the real world.
It follows logically from Descartes’s original decision to define the I as a thinking being—that is, as a thing, a “soul.”

If our I really is a “soul,” a thing-like being or “substance,” an unchanging hypokeimenon or underlying substance that remains beneath all our changes and actions, then like any other “thing” it must possess qualities that depend only on itself.
That means a human being’s qualities cannot depend on the natural world, including the body, or be constantly shaped through interaction with that world.

A soul shut up within itself therefore becomes infinitely poorer in qualities than a real human being, whose character is shaped by the immense variety of natural conditions in which life takes place.

From Descartes’s point of view, for example, Inuit people, Europeans, and Africans may live in very different ways because their bodies differ in certain respects. But everything genuinely human in them must be perfectly identical.
This leaves it impossible to explain why they differ not only in appearance but also in what they think and say.
If a human being is a “soul” or a “thing,” all of his essential qualities must be completely unchanging.

From Descartes’s point of view, there can therefore be no genuinely human difference between people living in ancient lake settlements and people living in American skyscrapers. Why the former do not think exactly like the latter becomes impossible to explain.

So this view strips human beings not only of the richness and variety produced by the different natural conditions in which they live, but also of the richness and variety produced by different historical conditions.
More generally, once philosophy defines the human I as a “soul-thing,” it is inevitably driven toward an extremely impoverished and simplified picture of humanity.

If we assume that the I is a “soul,” possessing from eternity unchanging qualities that belong only to itself—rather like the fixed properties of some perfectly tangible object—then only two possibilities remain.
Either all human beings are fundamentally identical, and the differences between them are merely superficial and have no real significance.
Or there are as many different “souls” as there are human beings.

But if every human being has a completely different soul, then the concept of “soul” loses all meaning. We might as well speak directly about living people. “Soul” would become nothing more than an extra, unnecessary word for a person.
And then there could be no general discourse or science of humanity—no anthropology.
We could speak only about isolated individuals.
Anything I could say about myself would interest no one except me, since it would apply to no one else.
Philosophy would then become a purely private and idle pastime.

But if, by contrast, we say that all human beings are essentially identical, we must either deny their physiological differences despite the obvious evidence, or declare those differences philosophically irrelevant.

And then everything that matters to actual flesh-and-blood human beings—intelligence and stupidity, decency and immorality, energy and apathy, political convictions, national differences, and so on—gets thrown overboard from the ship of “philosophy.”
Philosophy then becomes a “science” completely detached from life, one that ordinary people have no reason to care about.

If my philosophy—my answer to the question of who I am—is to have a genuinely common meaning and to interest other people, then the answers I give about myself must also tell us something about humanity in general.
Other people must be able to find in my answers something that helps them answer questions about themselves.
There must therefore be something common to human beings.
And philosophy must speak precisely about this common element.
But it has to be common in such a way that, by talking about it, philosophy can ultimately speak about each individual person, answering questions about each person’s own life.
Philosophy has always tried to give general answers to questions about the human I.

But if, like Descartes, we define the I as a “soul” or thing endowed with unchanging qualities, then the unchanging element supposedly common to all human beings becomes extraordinarily thin and abstract.
Such a philosophy gives a person answers that may be valid as far as they go, but remain obviously inadequate and unsatisfying: “a thinking being,” “a speaking being,” and so on.
Once all the differences produced by people’s lives in space and time are stripped away, what remains is something desperately poor, pale, and “abstract.”
No sensible person will recognize himself in it—or at least will not be satisfied by it.
This kind of abstraction characterizes almost all philosophy before Hegel.
And the reason I have spent so long on Descartes is precisely that he provides an excellent model of the pre-Hegelian way of philosophizing in general.
By studying him, we can see especially clearly why this philosophy fails.
Its failure comes from defining the human I as a kind of “soul” conceived in the image of natural things: something endowed with fixed qualities, given once and for all and dependent only on itself.

When it speaks about humanity in general, it must do so in a way that allows us to speak about every particular human being, helping each person answer questions about his or her real life in the real world.
That is precisely what Hegel managed to do when he broke with the traditional definition of the human I as a “thing” or “soul.”
Before turning to Hegel, however, we should draw together everything our discussion of Descartes has shown.
We must not begin from self-consciousness—from the fact that a human being speaks about what he is and uses the personal pronoun “I”—as though this were an inexplicable fact.
Why does self-consciousness exist at all? Why does a human being say “I”?
If we fail to ask this—if we ignore the question of the origin of the human I—we risk identifying that I with a “thing,” a “substance” endowed with unchanging “attributes.”

That, in turn, leads us to speak about humanity independently of its active relation to nature and history, while at the same time making it impossible to say anything about humanity without also invoking its imaginary relation to “God.”
On this view, knowing humanity does not require knowing everything, and answering questions about oneself does not require answering every possible question.
But the answers we get about humanity will necessarily remain inadequate.
They reveal only the most general and abstract human qualities, and give us no way to understand particular, concrete people.
If the problem is posed in this way, the goal of philosophy—“wisdom,” the ability to answer every question that can be asked of a human being about his life and actions—appears unattainable.
Now let us turn to Hegel
We can be much briefer here.
First, in criticizing Descartes we have already relied on many of Hegel’s central ideas.
Second, this entire book is devoted to explaining Hegelian ideas and the conclusions that follow from them.

The important point to notice again is that Hegel differs greatly from all his philosophical predecessors because he is not satisfied with abstract knowledge of humanity—claims such as “man is a thinking thing.”
He tries instead to answer the question of the concrete human being, and above all the question of himself.
His first major philosophical work, the Phenomenology, was in a sense written to give a complete and exact answer to Descartes’s question:
In this book Hegel appears, so to speak, in person. He explains what he is doing, why he is writing the book, and what he intends to do afterward.
In other words, he takes up the ancient philosophical demand to know oneself.
But he examines himself in such a way that the subject really is him—a concrete individual, not “humanity in general,” not an abstraction.
He speaks of himself as a human being living in a particular natural world, in a real country, at a definite moment in history.
So he explains not only how and why he thinks, but also how and why he writes and publishes what he writes.
Hegel completed the Phenomenology on the day of the Battle of Jena. On the very morning when, having written its final lines, he saw Napoleon riding beneath his windows.
So when Hegel answers the question “Who am I?”, those events form part of the answer.
Unlike earlier philosophers, he does not speak about some vague “human being in general,” living nowhere in particular, at no particular time, and doing nothing in particular.
He speaks about himself as a man living in Germany in 1807, at the height of Napoleon’s triumph, engaged in a very specific activity: writing the very book he actually wrote.
His answer to the question “Who am I?” is therefore genuinely concrete.
It is really about him, not about some abstract human being floating somewhere in the clouds with no definite personality.
What is remarkable, however, is that by answering concrete questions about his own concrete personality, Hegel also succeeded in answering the question of humanity in general.
His Phenomenology is therefore not only a philosophical autobiography. It is also a doctrine of humanity—an anthropology.
Anyone reading Hegel’s answers to questions about himself can use them to answer questions about themselves.
And those answers can remain just as concrete. They do not apply to an abstract “human being in general,” but to a particular person.
The element Hegel discovers as common to humanity is precisely the kind of commonality that necessarily takes concrete form in individual persons.
This is very different from the common features we find in things, where knowing what things have in common tells us almost nothing about what makes one individual thing different from another.
Hegel reached this result because he posed the question of himself in an entirely concrete way.

Unlike earlier philosophers, he did not want to deal with an abstraction. He did not try to “abstract away” from anything. He wanted to understand his concrete existence in all its fullness and richness.
That meant taking seriously the fact that he did not merely speak “in general,” but in particular said the word “I.”
Once he took this fact seriously, he turned it into a question.
And once he asked the question, he found the right answer.
He discovered the conditions without which the word “I” could never be spoken.
By discovering those conditions, he understood the origin of this speaking I—that is, the origin of self-consciousness.
And once he understood its origin, he could determine its character correctly.
He understood that the human I has nothing in common with what philosophy had traditionally called an immortal “soul” independent of the body.
